EverOS · voice support benchmark · τ²-bench telecom · interactive replay

Most voice agents start every call from the same playbook.

EverOS lets them learn from every call. A telecom support agent handled 74 calls; EverOS distilled them into skills — automatically. Facing 40 brand-new customers, the same agent with that experience resolved 62%. Without it: 50%. Every call below is real benchmark output — click any task to replay both calls side by side.

Success is judged by the benchmark's own environment assertions — the simulated phone must actually work at hang-up. Honest caveat: n = 40/arm; discordant pairs 6:1 (one-sided p ≈ 0.063) — directionally strong, below conventional significance. Both arms run gpt-4.1.

Before the fix, the lesson kept getting averaged away

EverOS consolidates per-call cases into agent-owned skills. Our first run (v1) exposed a real weakness: the consolidation step summarized the majority pattern and dropped the minority lesson from failed-then-corrected calls — the skill literally named "mobile data abroad" contained zero mentions of roaming. Four domain-agnostic rules later (contrastive, failure-derived insights must survive), the lesson sticks. Browse the actual files; roaming mentions are highlighted and counted.

The part we didn't hide

Our first run was a tie — and that's the best part of the story

v1: null result

Memory injection worked mechanically, yet resolution didn't move. Flip the arena above to "before fix" and see it.

Diagnosis

Of the both-fail tasks, 17 were "customer abroad" faults: the agent treated carrier-side roaming as proof the phone's own toggle was fine.

4

The fix

Four domain-agnostic consolidation rules. Zero telecom words — nothing about this benchmark leaks into the prompt.

+12pts

v2: verified

Same 74 calls replayed byte-identical; only the prompt changed. Wins landed exactly on the diagnosed family. Fix upstreamed.

The pattern generalizes to any support line — telecom is simply the domain with a rigorous public benchmark. All quantitative claims cite these τ²-bench telecom runs.

Technical notes — for whoever wires this in

The whole integration is four HTTP calls

Retrieve first, then let the model reason. The agent never "remembers" inside its own context window: it asks the memory layer, gets back distilled experience, and reasons over it. Everything below is what the benchmark actually ran — the code is in the repo, unabridged.

Standard agent — every call from zero
customer speaks
  ↓
policy + tools → LLM loop
  ↓
resolve · or give up → transfer
  ↓
hang up · nothing retained
Same agent, with EverOS
customer speaks
  ↓
search(agent_id, first utterance)
  ↓ skills + cases → <learned_experience>
policy + tools → LLM loop
  ↓ (optional) re-query with findings so far
resolve · or transfer
  ↓
hang up → add(call log) → flush
  ↓ background: episodes → cases → skills

step 1Memorize the call at hang-up

Post the transcript exactly as your telephony stack has it — roles, tool calls, timestamps. Scoping is carried by the ids on the request and on each message; there is no registration step. Then flush the session to hand it to extraction.

POST /api/v2/memory/add
{
  "session_id": "call-0421",                       // one per call
  "app_id": "voice-support", "project_id": "prod", // namespace + partition, your choice
  "messages": [
    {"sender_id": "support-agent", "role": "assistant", "content": "Hi! How can I help you today?", "timestamp": 1756000000000},
    {"sender_id": "cust-0421",     "role": "user",      "content": "My phone shows No Service since this morning…", "timestamp": 1756000015000},
    {"sender_id": "support-agent", "role": "assistant", "content": "", "timestamp": 1756000030000,
     "tool_calls": [{"id": "c1", "type": "function", "function": {"name": "get_customer_by_phone", "arguments": "{\"phone_number\": \"555-123-2002\"}"}}]},
    {"sender_id": "support-agent", "role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "c1", "content": "{\"customer_id\": \"C1001\", …}", "timestamp": 1756000036000}
    // … the rest of the call; failed/escalated calls end with the tier-2 close-out note
  ]
}
POST /api/v2/memory/flush   {"session_id": "call-0421", "app_id": "voice-support", "project_id": "prod", "messages": []}

step 2Retrieve when the next call starts

One search on the customer's first utterance. agent_id is simply the assistant sender_id you memorized under. The response is two lists — consolidated skills and the most similar past cases.

POST /api/v2/memory/search
{"agent_id": "support-agent", "app_id": "voice-support", "project_id": "prod",
 "query": "My phone shows No Service since this morning…",
 "method": "hybrid", "top_k": 5, "enable_llm_rerank": true}

→ {"data": {
     "agent_skills": [{"name": "Diagnose_and_fix_no_service_due_to_device_state",
                       "description": "…", "content": "## Steps\n1. …\n## Pitfalls\n- …", "confidence": 0.9}],
     "agent_cases":  [{"task_intent": "…", "approach": "…", "key_insight": "…", "quality_score": 0.9}]}}

step 3Render it into the system prompt — advisory, never authoritative

The benchmark agent is the stock τ²-bench LLMAgent plus this hook. Same model, same policy, same tools; the block is the only difference between the two arms.

EXPERIENCE_WRAPPER = """<learned_experience>
Operational experience distilled from your own previous support calls (across
many different customers). Use it to prioritize likely root causes and avoid
steps that historically did not help for this kind of issue. It is advisory:
always verify with live diagnostics and never violate the policy above.

{body}
</learned_experience>"""

class ExperienceAgent(LLMAgent):
    def generate_next_message(self, message, state):
        if self._is_first_customer_utterance(message):
            block = self._provider(message.content)            # the search above, rendered
            if block:
                self.experience_block = block
                state.system_messages = [SystemMessage(content=self.system_prompt)]
        return super().generate_next_message(message, state)

step 4Optionally re-query mid-call, on a fixed schedule

Opening utterances are vague ("my data doesn't work"). On the Nth customer turn the agent searches again with the opening symptom plus the grounded findings so far ("signal excellent, data on, still no connection, customer in France") and appends the result. The schedule is fixed per run — never conditioned on how the call is going — so the memory arm cannot cherry-pick when to consult memory. In this benchmark it fired on 28 of 40 calls.

between callsWhat EverOS does on its own

After every flush, in the background: an episode per customer, an agent case per call (intent / approach / key insight / quality score), then LLM clustering across cases into agent-owned skills. All of it lands as markdown you can open — the skills browser above is reading those files. One engineering note worth knowing: our first run showed consolidation averaging away the minority lessons carried by failed-then-corrected calls; the fix was four domain-agnostic rules in the consolidation prompt (contrastive, failure-derived insights must survive), which is what lifted 50% to 62%.

idwho sets itmeaning
app_id / project_idyou, per requestnamespace and partition — materialize as directories under the memory root
session_idyou, per requestone conversation; stream turns with repeated add, flush at hang-up
sender_id on user turnsyou, per messagebecomes a user-memory owner (users/<id>/) — customer-level memory, kept separate from the agent's
sender_id on assistant turnsyou, per messagebecomes the agent-memory owner (agents/<id>/) — this is where skills live
agent_id at searchyoumust equal the assistant sender_id
Isn't this just RAG over old transcripts?

No. Retrieval returns consolidated skills (procedures generalized across calls, with decision branches and pitfalls) plus a few case summaries — not raw transcript chunks. The consolidation step is what makes call #75 benefit from calls it never resembled word-for-word.

Does the memory arm see the benchmark's answers?

Never during evaluation. The only extra input is memory built from the disjoint training split. During learning, failed or escalated calls do receive the tier-2 close-out note (root cause + fix) — the same correction a real call center records when a human resolves an escalation.

Why the same model in both arms?

So the 12-point gap is attributable to memory alone. Model, temperature, policy, tools, max steps, seed and customer simulator are identical; the memory arm's only difference is the retrieved block.

How is "resolved" decided?

By τ²-bench's own environment assertions on the simulated phone at hang-up (e.g. mobile data on, speed test excellent). Not by us, not by an LLM judge. Handle time is modeled from event counts and labeled as such.

What changes in production?

Stream turns with repeated add calls during the call instead of one post at hang-up; put your gateway/auth in front of the server (EverOS binds loopback by default and ships no auth); and keep customer-level memory (users/) and agent-level memory (agents/) scoped as separate concerns — the benchmark deliberately used only the agent side.

Method & reproduction

Run it yourself

Benchmark — τ²-bench telecom (Sierra), dual-control: agent tools + guided device steps
Judge — the benchmark's environment assertions; never self-graded
Splits — 74 train / 40 test, disjoint; every test customer unseen
Arms — identical gpt-4.1 agent, policy, tools, seed, user simulator; only memory differs
Learning signal — full call logs; failed calls also get the tier-2 ticket close-out note
Cost — ≈ $23 full experiment (~$0.12 per simulated call)

Code, data, and this page: github.com/JadeeeZh/everos-voice-support. Want to feel the memory layer before running the benchmark? The hands-on walkthrough installs EverOS from PyPI, feeds twelve real calls one request at a time, and shows the skill forming on disk — about twenty minutes, under a dollar.

git clone https://github.com/JadeeeZh/everos-voice-support && cd everos-voice-support
make setup                 # vendors τ²-bench (pinned), installs the everos CLI, syncs the venv
echo 'OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-…' > .env
make smoke                 # 3 learning + 2 eval calls, end-to-end (~$1)
make learn RUN=v1 && make evaluate RUN=v1 && make report RUN=v1   # the full experiment (~$23)
